title: What Is MCP & Why It Exists
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting agents to tools and data. Instead of hand-writing a bespoke integration for every tool, an agent (the client, inside a host app) speaks one protocol to any MCP server, which exposes its capabilities in a uniform way. It's the 'USB-C for tools': one connector, many devices.

subtopics.title: The M×N integration problem
subtopics.explanation: Without a standard, every agent (M of them) needs custom glue code to talk to every tool or data source (N of them), giving you M×N brittle integrations to build and maintain. Each provider invents its own auth, argument shapes, and error formats, so nothing is reusable. MCP collapses this to M+N by putting one shared protocol between agents and tools, which is the entire reason the standard exists.
subtopics.example:
# WITHOUT a standard: bespoke glue per (agent, tool) pair
def call_github(agent_ctx):
    # custom auth, custom request shape, custom error parsing
    ...

def call_slack(agent_ctx):
    # a DIFFERENT auth, shape, and errors -- nothing reused
    ...

# add a 3rd agent and a 4th tool -> you rewrite ALL the glue.
# M agents x N tools = M*N integrations to maintain.

subtopics.title: MCP as the 'USB-C for tools'
subtopics.explanation: USB-C standardized one physical connector so any laptop can talk to any monitor, drive, or charger without a drawer full of adapters. MCP plays the same role for agents: a single protocol lets any MCP-speaking agent connect to any MCP server — a database, a file system, a SaaS API — with no custom adapter. The analogy matters because it reframes tool access from 'a coding project per tool' to 'plug in a compliant server.'
subtopics.example:
# WITH MCP: one client speaks ONE protocol to any server
client = MCPClient()

# same code path, different servers -- like plugging into USB-C
client.connect("github-server")   # exposes issues, PRs, repos
client.connect("postgres-server") # exposes query, schema
client.connect("files-server")    # exposes read, write, list

# the agent discovers each server's tools the SAME way
tools = client.list_tools()  # uniform shape, no per-tool glue

subtopics.title: Host, client, and server roles
subtopics.explanation: MCP defines three roles. The host is the application the user runs (an IDE, a chat app, a desktop assistant). Inside it, a client is the connection manager that maintains one session per server. A server is a separate process that exposes tools, data, and prompts. Keeping these roles distinct is what lets one host manage many independent servers safely, each in its own process.
subtopics.example:
# HOST: the app the user interacts with (e.g. an IDE or chat app)
#   +-- CLIENT: one per server connection, owns the session
#   |     +--> SERVER A (github): tools = create_issue, ...
#   |     +--> SERVER B (postgres): tools = run_query, ...
#
# The host launches clients; each client speaks MCP to one server.
host = ChatApp()
client_gh = host.new_client()
client_gh.connect("github-server")   # 1 client <-> 1 server session

subtopics.title: Servers expose tools, resources, and prompts
subtopics.explanation: An MCP server doesn't just offer functions to call. It advertises three kinds of capability: tools (actions the model can invoke), resources (readable data like files or rows the model can pull into context), and prompts (reusable templates the host can surface to the user). A client discovers all three at connect time. Understanding that a server exposes data and templates — not only actions — is what separates MCP from a plain function-calling API.
subtopics.example:
# A server advertises its capabilities when a client connects.
capabilities = {
    "tools":     ["search_docs", "create_ticket"],  # actions to invoke
    "resources": ["file:///readme.md", "db://orders"],  # data to read
    "prompts":   ["summarize_thread", "triage_bug"],   # templates to fill
}
# the client lists each category with a uniform discovery call.
# NOTE: exact method names vary by SDK version; the shape is stable.

subtopics.title: Why a standard beats bespoke integrations
subtopics.explanation: A shared protocol means a server built once works with every compliant host, and a host gains new capabilities just by pointing at a new server — no code change on either side. Ecosystems compound: tool authors publish servers, app authors consume them, and both sides innovate independently. That decoupling — write once, connect anywhere — is precisely the leverage a standard provides over one-off integrations.
subtopics.example:
# One server, many hosts -- write it once, reuse everywhere.
# server.py published by a tool author:
#   exposes tool `run_query` over MCP

# Host A (an IDE) and Host B (a chat app) both connect with
# ZERO server changes -- they just speak MCP:
ide_client.connect("analytics-server")
chat_client.connect("analytics-server")
# new host tomorrow? it connects too, no new glue code.

foundations.overview: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that defines how an AI agent connects to external tools and data. Before it, wiring a model to a tool meant bespoke code for each pairing — custom auth, argument formats, and error handling — so a system with several agents and several tools drowned in M×N brittle integrations. MCP inserts one shared protocol between the two sides. A host application runs one or more clients; each client opens a session with a server; and the server advertises its capabilities as tools (actions), resources (data), and prompts (templates). Because every server speaks the same protocol, any compliant host can use any compliant server without new glue — the 'USB-C for tools' idea. The intelligence still lives in the model and the agent loop; MCP is the connective tissue that makes tool and data access reusable, discoverable, and decoupled, which is why it matters as agents move from demos into real, multi-tool systems.
foundations.formalDefinition: MCP is an open client-server protocol in which a host application instantiates clients that each maintain a stateful session with a server; the server exposes capabilities in three categories — tools (invocable actions), resources (readable context data), and prompts (parameterized templates) — over a standardized message format, so any conforming client can discover and use any conforming server without custom integration code.
foundations.whyItMatters: As agents gain access to more systems, the cost of integration — not model quality — becomes the bottleneck. A standard turns O(M×N) bespoke connectors into O(M+N) reusable ones, lets tool authors and app authors ship independently, and gives users a growing catalog of pluggable capabilities, which is what makes multi-tool agents practical to build and maintain.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of MCP like USB-C. Your laptop (the host) doesn't need a different port for every device; it has one connector, and any compliant device — a monitor, a drive, a charger — just works. An MCP server is such a device: plug it in and the host discovers what it offers. You stop writing an adapter per tool and start plugging in servers.
foundations.realWorldUsage: IDE assistants connecting to file-system, git, and database servers; chat and desktop assistants pulling in company knowledge-base and ticketing servers; and internal platforms publishing one MCP server per system so any approved agent can use it without new integration work.
commonUseCases: Giving an agent access to files, databases, or APIs without bespoke glue
Publishing an internal system once as a reusable MCP server
Letting one host app connect to many independent tool servers
Sharing community/vendor servers across different agent hosts

commonMisconceptions.myth: MCP is an Anthropic-only or single-vendor feature.
commonMisconceptions.reality: MCP is an open protocol with a public specification and multiple SDKs; any host or server author can implement it, and servers work across different clients.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An MCP server only exposes functions to call.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Servers expose three capability types — tools (actions), resources (readable data), and prompts (templates). Reducing it to 'just functions' misses resources and prompts.

commonMisconceptions.myth: MCP replaces the agent loop or the model.
commonMisconceptions.reality: MCP is connective tissue for tool and data access, not an agent framework. The reasoning still comes from the model inside its loop; MCP just standardizes how it reaches tools.

checkpoints.prompt: What core problem does MCP primarily solve?
options: The M×N explosion of bespoke agent-to-tool integrations
checkpoints.explanation: Without a standard, M agents each need custom glue for N tools (M×N integrations). MCP puts one shared protocol between them, reducing it to M+N reusable pieces. It doesn't change how the model reasons.

checkpoints.prompt: In MCP's role model, what is the 'host'?
options: The application the user runs, which manages clients
checkpoints.explanation: The host is the user-facing application (an IDE, chat app, or assistant). It instantiates clients, and each client maintains a session with one server. The server is a separate process exposing capabilities.

checkpoints.prompt: Which trio of capabilities does an MCP server expose?
checkpoints.explanation: A server advertises tools (invocable actions), resources (readable context data such as files or rows), and prompts (reusable parameterized templates). Reducing MCP to 'just functions' misses resources and prompts.

keyTakeaways: MCP is an open standard that connects agents to tools and data through one shared protocol instead of bespoke integrations.
It turns the M×N integration explosion into M+N: write a server once, and any compliant host can use it.
The 'USB-C for tools' analogy captures the shift — one connector, many pluggable capabilities, no per-tool adapters.
MCP has three roles: a host app runs clients, each client opens a session with a server that exposes capabilities.
Servers expose tools (actions), resources (readable data), and prompts (templates) — not just functions to call.
